description: Keynotes talks from BSides Las Vegas 2024.

talks.title: Closing Ceremony
talks.teaser: Wraps up BSides Las Vegas 2024 with attendance figures, CTF awards, and a charity auction.
talks.summary:
The closing ceremony of BSides Las Vegas 2024 opens with organizers reviewing the year. They report roughly 490 talk proposals, about 200 talks and trainings across ten tracks, and new formats such as facilitated discussion groups. Feedback on the keynotes was positive, and the organizers welcomed a new partnership with Sky Talks. They also noted scheduling lessons for next year, including not booking a keynote speaker straight into another session.

The middle of the ceremony is devoted to contests. The instructor of a cloud forensics training describes the mini capture-the-flag run during the course and hands out challenge coins and a learning subscription to the top individual and team finishers. The organizer of an offensive and defensive exercise then explains its format: a red team with weeks of advance access to a simulated enterprise network, including Active Directory and web servers, faces blue teams that spend days preparing to detect and hunt. The exercise ends with a scorched-earth phase and a hot wash in which the red team explains its techniques and the defenders' options. The winning team is announced, and the staff and players are thanked.

The final segment covers a charity auction that raised just over $10,000 for two supported charities, with the organizers announcing that BSides would round the total up. Unsold items went into a lucky-loser raffle. The organizers close by asking attendees to raise their hands if they met someone new, learned something, or plan to act on something they picked up at the event, and they send the audience off to return next year.

talks.title: "Secure AI" is 20 years old
talks.teaser: Traces two decades of machine learning security history and argues defenders should plan for fast response over perfect models.
talks.summary:
Sven Cattell opens with the claim that machine learning security is much older than the current generative AI wave, pointing to a spam-filter bypass documented in 2004 as an early example. He argues that many people now calling themselves AI red teamers lack this history, and that some work labeled red teaming, such as brand-safety filtering or bias testing, has no real adversary behind it.

The middle of the talk draws lessons from years of production spam and malware classifiers. Models are never perfect, attackers keep finding inputs outside the training distribution, and features that users can easily manipulate tend to fail. Cattell describes a malware detector whose allowlist was bypassed by appending data to a trusted game binary, and a social network that limited exposure by training models on random feature subsets and redeploying them frequently. He also treats adversarial-example defenses with skepticism and argues that data poisoning is rarely economical against large production systems.

He closes with a framework: assume a model will eventually be bypassed, ask whether a control buys time or speeds response, and invest in detection and fast redeployment. For language models, he suggests treating prompt injection and information leakage like the older problems, applying classifiers and layered controls, and learning from the people who already attack these systems.

talks.title: Homicideware
talks.teaser: Uses historical engineering catastrophes and the Y2K and Melissa episodes to argue for safety-based computer security policy.
talks.summary:
Matwyshyn opens with the 25th anniversary of the Y2K remediation effort and the Melissa virus, which the FBI described as foreshadowing modern threats. She argues that computer security policy and legal thinking have not caught up. Outages now cause large financial losses and can threaten public safety, critical infrastructure and national security, yet the field still frames much of the problem narrowly around confidentiality breaches.

The middle of the talk presents early research on more than 120 engineering catastrophes that involved deaths. She identifies recurring failure patterns, including unaddressed technical debt, ignored warnings, designs that assume flawless human operation, neglected maintenance, rushed schedules and changing conditions. A 1919 Boston molasses tank collapse illustrates how a known defect was concealed and how the resulting liability reshaped engineering practice. She contrasts this with the Y2K response, which passed two statutes, narrowed liability, excluded physical injury claims and let judges appoint technical experts. The recent CrowdStrike update disruption serves as a current example of how an availability failure can be treated as a safety emergency.

She argues that courts will judge incidents by context, harm and knowledge, meaning what a person in a given role should have known, not only what they admit knowing. Market forces alone will not fix this, she says, so she proposes a dedicated technology safety body with enforcement, policy coordination, foresight and pilot functions. For practitioners, the takeaway is to threat model foreseeable failures and to explain security work in terms that non-specialists understand.
